clips.title: Segregation of Duties
clips.why: Accountants solved this problem long ago: the person who asks for a payment must not be the person who approves it.
look: Which duties must be held by different people, and why one person holding two of them invites mistakes and fraud.
How the examples map to ours: asking for the work, writing it, and approving it.
That the control works even when everyone is honest, because it also catches honest mistakes.
clips.after: Our requester set is segregation of duties for pull requests: whoever asked, wrote or edited the change cannot be the one who approves it.

clips.title: Introduction To GitHub Actions: Part 8 - Pull Request Workflow
clips.why: A clear look at the trigger settings of a pull request workflow, which decide when a check like ours runs again.
look: The activity types a pull_request trigger can listen for, such as opened and synchronize.
What happens when a workflow does not list a type: that event never re-runs it.
Think about which events must re-run an approval check: a new commit, an edited description, a new review.
clips.after: fcp's caller listens to pull_request (opened, edited, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review) and pull_request_review (submitted, edited, dismissed), so every change that matters re-runs the check.

clips.title: Stop Rubber-Stamping Your AI: Human-in-the-Loop UIs in Claude (Case Study)
clips.why: A short warning about review queues that turn into rubber stamps when people approve AI output without looking.
look: Why a review that is easy to give and hard to refuse slowly becomes a formality.
That the person approving should not be the person who wants the output most.
clips.after: The check makes sure the one approval comes from someone outside the request; the evidence in Nova's pull request is what makes that review quick and real.

clips.title: Your Code Review Process Is Lying to You
clips.why: Two minutes on automated gates in front of review, and on who owns code that an AI wrote.
look: Which checks a machine should run before a person reviews anything.
His point about ownership of AI-written code: a named person answers for it.
clips.after: In our platform the requester owns the work and an independent person approves it; the machine only checks that those are two different people.

practice.q: PR #2512's body ends with Requested-by: @sean. Who is in the requester set if only Nova pushed commits and nobody edited the body?

options.why: The author is in the set too, here the agents' bot account.
The author plus the Requested-by login. Pushers and body editors would join them if there were any.

options.text: Everyone who reviewed the pull request.
options.why: Reviewers are who the check judges, not who it excludes, unless they also pushed or edited the body.

practice.q: Finish the filter so approvals from apps and bots never count.
practice.hint: GitHub's type for a person's account.
practice.why: GitHub marks a person's account as User and an app's as Bot, so Byte's approval is filtered out here.

practice.q: Dana approved the head commit, then later left a plain comment: "one small nit, fine to merge". Does her approval still count?

options.text: Yes. A comment is not a decisive review, so her latest decisive review is still the approval.
options.why: Only APPROVED, CHANGES_REQUESTED and DISMISSED replace an earlier decision.

options.text: No. Her latest review is now a comment.
options.why: That would let a friendly comment silently cancel an approval. The check ignores plain comments.

options.text: No. Any activity after an approval resets it.
options.why: Only a new commit (and a new decisive review) changes the picture.

practice.q: Put the check's decision in order, from reading the pull request to the result.
items: Read the author and the Requested-by line, and fail if an agent PR has none
Add every commit author and every body editor to the requester set
Keep each reviewer's latest decisive review
Keep only approvals on the head commit, from users, outside the requester set
Pass if at least one is left, otherwise fail
practice.why: First decide who may not approve, then look at the approvals, then decide.

practice.q: A routine's pull request has no Requested-by line because of a bug in the orchestrator. What should the check do?

options.text: Pass, because any approval from a person is better than none.
options.why: Then the easiest way around the check would be to drop the line.

options.text: Treat the routine's owner as the requester by looking them up in the charter.
options.why: The check does not guess. The line is the contract between the orchestrator and the check.

options.text: Fail with a clear message, so a person sees the bug and fixes the pull request.
options.why: Failing closed: when the check cannot tell who asked, it says no.
